message.content: The number of mitochondria in a cell is not fixed—it varies widely depending on the cell type and its energy demands. In most mammalian cells, you’ll find somewhere between a few dozen to several hundred mitochondria per cell. Highly active cells, such as cardiac myocytes or skeletal muscle fibers, can contain thousands of mitochondria to meet their high ATP requirements. Conversely, cells with lower metabolic rates may have fewer mitochondria. Thus, while there isn’t a single “number” that applies to all cells, a typical range is roughly **50–500 mitochondria per cell**, with extremes reaching up to several thousand in specialized tissues.
